title: Progress On TriageNet
content:
Phase 3 of TriageNet is officially complete! 🚀

After laying the foundation in Phase 1 & 2, today was all about bringing the Java core backend engine to life and building real-world clinical safety logic into the system.

Here’s what got built in Phase 3:

🧠 Java Algorithmic Core:
Ported our ML Severity Scorer into Java Spring Boot (complete with explainable risk factor breakdowns and automatic sepsis alerts), alongside Dijkstra's algorithm for regional referral routes and the Hungarian algorithm for multi-resource bed matching.

🔒 Non-Preemptible Critical Occupancy Locks:
What happens if a specialty hospital’s ICU beds are 100% full of critical patients? You can’t kick out a critical ICU patient. The AI engine now detects this "critical lock" and automatically performs a temporary emergency holding assignment at a nearby facility to avoid waiting-room casualties.

🛏️ Bed Stratification & Disease-Specific Recovery Timelines:
Beds are now split into dedicated ICU vs. General Ward pools. Different conditions now have customized recovery thresholds — so a severe respiratory patient stays in ICU until SpO₂ stabilizes, while a trauma patient follows a different step-down timeline before being automatically shifted to a General Ward bed.

💊 Automatic Bed Releases & On-Call Doctor Rosters:
When a patient is discharged, the system frees their bed in real time (marked with a green status badge) and immediately auto-assigns the freed bed to the top waiting candidate. Plus, each hospital now tracks on-call doctor availability for Pulmonologists, Cardiologists, and Trauma Surgeons.

🎨 Accessibility & High-Contrast Overhaul:
Cleaned up the UI contrast across system alerts, simulation controls, and status badges so clinical operators can read everything at a glance during high-stress simulation runs.

All 8 Java test suites passed with 100% success, and the full codebase is pushed to GitHub!

Next up: Phase 4 — End-to-end API integration connecting the Next.js frontend to the Java backend endpoints.

title: Building TriageNet — When Algorithms Meet Healthcare
content:
My most complex project yet just hit a major milestone. TriageNet is an 
AI-powered hospital triage and resource optimization system I'm building 
as my final year project at AEC — and it's unlike anything I've built before.

The idea: connect 4 regional hospitals in a weighted graph network, then 
use algorithms to automatically route patients to the right facility in 
real time. Not just the nearest hospital — the one with the right beds, 
the right equipment, and the right specialist available. All three 
conditions have to match before any assignment happens.

Under the hood: a Logistic Regression ML model scores patient severity 
from 0–100 using clinical vitals (SpO₂, heart rate, blood pressure, 
temperature, respiratory rate, age). Dijkstra's algorithm finds the 
shortest-path referral route. The Hungarian algorithm handles optimal 
bed assignment. And if SpO₂ drops below 90% with HR above 110 bpm, the 
system fires a sepsis early warning automatically.

Phase 1 and 2 are done — all 12 operational dashboard pages are live, 
the ML engine is running, and the Spring Boot backend with JWT auth and 
Docker Compose is scaffolded. Now comes the hardest part: wiring the 
backend algorithms to the frontend in real time.

This one's going to the final year presentation. Building it in public.
